opus-5.5.text:
I think Yann's direction is a very reasonable one, and in some sense it addresses something that the current mainstream, the large language model paradigm, doesn't fully solve. His core argument is that predicting the next token in text isn't enough to build an agent that truly understands the world. Humans and animals learn a huge amount just by observing, before they ever use language. A baby learns object permanence and intuitive physics without anyone telling them in words. So the question is how to get a machine to learn that kind of predictive model of the world.

What I find interesting about his approach, especially the JEPA line of work, the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, is that he doesn't try to predict every pixel. If you try to generate the next frame of a video pixel by pixel, you waste a lot of capacity modeling details that don't matter, like the exact texture of leaves blowing in the wind. Instead, you predict in a learned representation space, an abstract space where the irrelevant noise has been filtered out. I think that's an important insight, because a good world model should capture the structure that matters for planning and decision-making, not every surface detail.

That said, I think there are still a lot of open questions. One is how you make sure the representation doesn't collapse. If you're only predicting in latent space, the trivial solution is to map everything to the same point, and then prediction is perfect but useless. There's been a lot of work, including some of my own earlier theoretical work on self-supervised learning, trying to understand why these non-contrastive methods don't collapse in practice. The dynamics are quite subtle. So the theory isn't fully settled yet.

The second question is scaling. Language models showed that if you have a simple objective and a lot of data and compute, you get surprising capabilities. For world models, we haven't yet seen that same kind of clean scaling story where you just add more video and the model suddenly learns to plan and reason. Maybe it will come, but it's not obvious yet.

And third, I personally think the two directions aren't necessarily in opposition. Language is a very compressed representation of human knowledge, and LLMs have absorbed a lot of world knowledge through text. A world model learned from perception could provide the grounding, and language could provide the abstraction and reasoning. Eventually I suspect a strong system will combine both: a model that can imagine what happens if it takes an action, and a model that can reason symbolically about goals and plans. Planning, search, and reasoning are things I've worked on for a long time, and to me a world model is essentially what makes planning possible. You can't search over futures if you can't predict them.

So overall, I respect that Yann has a clear, long-term vision and is willing to go against the mainstream. Research needs people doing that. Whether JEPA specifically is the final answer, I don't know, but the problem he's pointing at, learning predictive, abstract models of the world from observation, is definitely one of the key problems we need to solve.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes LeCun’s approach as going against the mainstream and says key questions remain open, including whether world models have a clear scaling path, framing it as an important direction still to be explored.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Yann is asking the right question, even if I don't think anyone, including him, has the final answer yet.

His core argument is that autoregressive language models are fundamentally limited. They predict the next token, they don't really understand the physical world, they don't plan, and they can't learn from a few observations the way a child does. His proposal is JEPA, the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, where instead of predicting pixels or tokens you predict in an abstract representation space, and you let the model decide what details are worth predicting and what details are noise. I find that idea very appealing. If you force a model to reconstruct every leaf on a tree, you waste capacity on things that don't matter for decisions. Predicting in latent space is the right level of abstraction for planning.

Where I'm more cautious is on the engineering side. Large language models work partly because the objective is dead simple and scales beautifully. Joint embedding methods have a collapse problem, the representation can become trivial, and you need regularizers like VICReg or careful architecture tricks to prevent that. Those tricks have worked at the scale of ImageNet and video clips. Whether they work at the scale where LLMs operate, that's still an open empirical question. I-JEPA and V-JEPA are promising, but they're not yet showing the kind of emergent capability jump that convinced everyone about scaling language models.

I'd also push back a little on the framing that it's one or the other. Language is a compressed world model that humans already built over thousands of years. Throwing that away seems wasteful. My personal view is that the eventual system looks hybrid. You want something that learns dynamics from perception, in the JEPA spirit, but you also want to leverage the enormous prior that's encoded in text. And honestly, some of the planning and search ideas that Yann puts in the "world model plus cost module" box are things people are already bolting onto LLMs, tree search, verifiers, learned value functions. The boundaries are blurrier than the debates on Twitter suggest.

So in short, I agree with the diagnosis, I like the direction, and I think the field benefits from someone with his stature refusing to accept that next-token prediction is the end of the story. But I treat it as a research bet, not a settled roadmap. The proof will be a system that plans in an unfamiliar environment better than a scaled transformer does, and we haven't seen that yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes JEPA as promising but says its scalability is an open empirical question, calls it a research bet rather than a settled roadmap, and says the proof has not yet been seen.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what does a model need to understand in order to act intelligently? Predicting the next word is one way to learn about the world, but if you want a system to plan, it also needs some ability to predict the consequences of its actions.

A world model could let the system ask, “If I do this, what is likely to happen? And does that bring me closer to my goal?” It doesn’t necessarily need to predict every detail. If you’re moving a cup across a table, you care about where the cup will end up and whether it will fall, not the exact appearance of every pixel.

The difficult part is learning which details matter. That depends on the task, and a model can make small prediction errors that become much larger when you plan several steps ahead. So learning a useful representation and making it reliable enough for planning are closely connected problems.

I see this as a promising direction, but I wouldn’t frame it as a choice between language models and world models. Language can provide knowledge and help describe goals; a world model can help evaluate possible actions. The interesting question is how to make those capabilities work together.

r001.rationale: The response calls world models a promising direction, but does not say that this research direction is insufficiently explored.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very interesting direction. The central question is how a model can learn enough about the world to predict the consequences of its actions and use those predictions to plan. Language gives us a lot of knowledge, but it doesn’t necessarily give us that capability by itself.

One important idea in Yann’s approach is that you don’t need to predict every detail of a future observation. If you’re watching a car turn a corner, predicting the exact appearance of every pixel may be less useful than understanding where the car is going. So the challenge is to learn a representation that preserves what matters for prediction and decision-making.

But that raises a difficult question: what matters? You need to retain enough information to support different tasks, while leaving out details that are unpredictable or irrelevant. And even if you learn a good predictive model, turning it into a reliable planner is another substantial challenge.

So I see it as a promising research direction, with important open problems. I also think world models and language models can complement each other. Language can help specify goals and communicate knowledge, while a world model can help evaluate what might happen when you act.

r001.rationale: The response calls the direction promising and mentions open problems, but does not clearly characterize it as insufficiently explored.
